name: LeMonHash
baseline: Hollow Trie / Centroid Hollow Trie / ZFast Trie / PaCo Trie (prior state-of-the-art monotone minimal perfect hash function techniques); functionally these replace a sorted-array binary search or std::map rank query
workload: Rank queries (monotone minimal perfect hashing) over synthetic 64-bit integer datasets (uniform/normal/exponential, 100M keys) and real-world datasets (text, dna, urls, 5gram, fb, osm; 35M-800M keys), measuring query throughput, construction throughput, and bits/key vs prior MMPHF techniques
claimed_speedup: About 16x faster queries at 34% less space than the next larger competitor on synthetic integer data; up to 19x faster queries on real-world data at similar space; up to 2x faster construction than the next-best-space competitor (Hollow Trie variants); LeMonHash-VL (string variant) achieves up to 3x faster queries than the next larger competitor within 13% of its space
hardware: Intel Xeon E5-2670 v3 @ 2.3GHz, Ubuntu 20.04, Linux 5.10.0, single-threaded
tradeoffs: GPLv3 is copyleft (no permissive reuse in proprietary code); like all MPHFs it returns arbitrary output for keys outside the original set; monotone MPHFs preserve key order (unlike plain MPHFs), which is a narrower guarantee that costs more space than a non-order-preserving MPHF; needs epsilon tuning for the PGM bucket mapper and depends on the BuRR retrieval structure and PGM-index as building blocks
caveats: Competitors benchmarked include Java implementations run on OpenJDK with JIT warm-up (author's own comparison notes Java is expected to be close to C++ performance, per prior work); comparison is against academic MMPHF implementations, not against std::map/std::unordered_map directly; each experiment run only twice and averaged (paper states variation is small)
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "MPHF" --sort stars -> ByteHamster/LeMonHash; cross-checked against arXiv:2304.11012 (ESA 2023)

name: Sphinx
baseline: DHT (Delta Hash Table, a dynamic perfect hash table) / RSQF / Aleph Filter / Adaptive Aleph Filter (state-of-the-art fingerprint and perfect-hash indexes for log-structured hash tables / key-value stores)
workload: Average and tail-99 query/update/insertion latency and memory footprint (bits/entry) of an in-memory, Optane, and SSD-resident LSH-table index over up to 10^8 keys, against DHT, DHT-expandable, RSQF, Aleph Filter and Adaptive Aleph Filter C++ implementations
claimed_speedup: About 2x reduction in query latency, update latency, and memory footprint vs. the best alternative baseline (paper abstract); zero false positives (vs. RSQF/Aleph Filter's growing FPR); lowest average and tail-99 latency across in-memory, Optane and SSD experiments (Figures 8-9)
hardware: Platform 1: Intel Xeon W7-2495X (24 cores/48 threads, 2.5GHz), 1.9MB L1/48MB L2/45MB L3, 512GB NVMe SSD (OS) + 2TB Samsung 980 Pro SSD (benchmark drive), Ubuntu 22.04; Platform 2: dual Intel Xeon Silver 4314 (32 cores/64 threads, 2.4GHz) with 256GB RAM + 496GB Intel Optane Persistent Memory 200 Series, Ubuntu 22.04
stars_or_usage: 22 stars; VLDB 2025 paper (PVLDB vol. 18) with ACM 'Artifacts Available' badge
tradeoffs: Designed specifically as an in-memory index for LSH-table / log-structured key-value stores (not a general-purpose associative container); relies on x86 rank/select instructions (POPCNT, PEXT, TZCNT) for full speed; static succinct trie-based decoder is built for a fixed key set per block and expands via block-group splitting rather than arbitrary rehashing; DHT baseline was the authors' own C++ re-implementation since the original DHT code is closed-source
caveats: CPU model and platform are stated but exact compiler version and optimization flags were not found in the sections of the paper reviewed, so capped at Tier B rather than A; baselines are DHT/RSQF/Aleph Filter, not std::unordered_map or CMPH/BBHash directly, so this is an indirect (not literal) hit on the assigned incumbent list
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "perfect hash" --sort stars -> sfmqrb/sphinx; cross-checked against VLDB 2025 paper p4424-maghrebi.pdf

name: entropy-map
baseline: std::unordered_map / Rust std::collections::HashMap (general-purpose hash map; entropy-map markets itself as an ultra-low-latency hash-map replacement built on a minimal perfect hash function)
workload: Lookup latency and memory footprint of an immutable Rust hash map/set built on a fingerprinting-based MPHF (inspired by the beling/bsuccinct-rs 'ph' crate), configurable via group-size and gamma parameters; exact key count/type for the quoted numbers is not stated in the README
claimed_speedup: Query time ranging from 5ns to 20ns depending on parameters, key count and L1-L3 cache sizes; memory usage from 2.10 to 2.71 bits per key depending on parameters (README 'Overview' section; absolute numbers, no head-to-head timing table against a baseline shown on this page)
stars_or_usage: 45 stars; developed and used by Cloudflare
tradeoffs: Immutable map/set only (no post-construction inserts); Rust crate, so C++ use requires an FFI boundary; requires a value dictionary (MapWithDict) for arbitrary values rather than native insert semantics; construction-time vs. query-time tradeoff tunable via a gamma parameter
caveats: The README states absolute ns/bits-per-key numbers without a comparison table, hardware, or compiler details, so this is a first-party (Tier C) claim; it cites being 'inspired by' and improving construction/query times over the 'ph' crate (part of beling/bsuccinct-rs, which is already on the known list) but does not quantify that specific comparison anywhere on the page reviewed; baseline (std::HashMap-equivalent) is inferred per the 'hash map obviously targets std::unordered_map' rule, so confidence is capped
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "MPHF" --sort stars -> cloudflare/entropy-map

name: MQF (Mixed-counters Quotient Filter)
workload: Query time for 35 million existing real k-mers looked up in MQF filters loaded to 60%, 70%, 80% and 90% capacity, with MQF's per-key 'label' feature used as a minimal perfect hash function and compared against BBHash-style MPHFs
claimed_speedup: ~10-fold faster query time than BBHash (MPHFs), with MQF query time reported as invariable across load factors (paper Additional file 1, Figure S6; abstract states "the labels serve as a minimal perfect hash function but are ~10 fold faster than BBhash")
hardware: AWS t3.large instance (2 vCPUs, 8GB RAM), Ubuntu Server 18.04 (exact CPU model not specified; burstable cloud instance type)
stars_or_usage: 12 stars; published in BMC Bioinformatics 22:71 (2021), used in k-mer/genomics counting pipelines from the dib-lab group
tradeoffs: MQF is fundamentally a dynamic counting/labeling quotient filter (supports insert/remove/resize/merge) rather than a pure static MPHF like BBHash, so the 'perfect hash' behavior is one feature (label lookup) of a broader data structure, not a drop-in MPHF replacement; a buffered/disk-backed variant trades speed for memory; comparison hardware is a shared/burstable cloud VM rather than a dedicated bare-metal benchmark box
caveats: Speedup is reported as an aggregate '~10 fold' claim tied to a supplementary figure (Additional file 1, Fig. S6) rather than a detailed per-configuration numeric table; exact CPU model and compiler/optimization flags are not stated, so this is capped at Tier B despite being a peer-reviewed journal paper; the GitHub project has not been updated since October 2023
found_via: WebSearch: 'MQF minimal perfect hash function k-mer "10 fold faster" BBHash github' -> dib-lab/MQF; cross-checked against BMC Bioinformatics paper via PMC (PMC7885209)
